Create a weight model for selection within rate cells

Source: R/weight_model.R
weight_model.Rd

Create a weight_model that will be used to generate weights for determining which individuals/units experience an event.

Usage

weight_model(formula = NULL, coefficients = numeric(), fun = NULL)

Arguments

formula

A one-sided formula of weight variables.

coefficients

A finite named numeric vector of log hazard ratios.

fun

A custom function returning log weights, instead of formula.

Value

A hammel_weight_model. This specifies a model; it does not estimate one.

Details

A weight model decides which member of a rate cell experiences an event, without changing the cell's input intensity and thus the input rates. The cell produces events at its input rate times its members; each event goes to member i with probability w_i / sum(w), where w_i = exp(eta_i).

With a formula, eta_i is the linear predictor x_i %*% beta, so exp(beta) is the hazard ratio between two members of the same cell that differ by one unit in a term. Users can therefore create proportional hazards models, without affecting overall input rates. Population level effects can be smaller where cells are small or homogeneous.

Attach a weight model with the weights argument of set_mortality(), set_fertility(), set_union_dissolution(), set_group_transition() and set_union_formation(), or weights_conversion of set_union_formation().

Variables

Group variables are named by the declared group dimensions (see set_groups()); for a dimension race with categories A and B.

Mortality, fertility and group transitions are person processes and may use sex ("f", "m"), race, union_type ("unpartnered", "cohab", "marriage"), partnered (0/1), parity (births; 0 for men), previous_union ("none", "separated", "widowed"), partner_race (NA when unpartnered) and, when the dimension tracks ancestry, shares ancestry_race_A and ancestry_race_unknown. Group transitions may also use destination, the destination of the risk in the transition's dimension.

Dissolution and conversion are union processes and may use race_w, race_h, parity_w, previous_union_w, previous_union_h, ancestry_race_A_w, ancestry_race_A_h, same_race (0/1), age_difference (husband's age minus wife's age) and union_type ("cohab", "marriage").

The first listed level of each categorical variable is its reference; for a group dimension it is its first category (declared, or first in the population).

Formulas

Terms are main effects of these variables and interactions (: or *); transformations such as I() are not supported (use fun). Categorical variables use treatment coding, and coefficients must be named exactly as the corresponding model-matrix columns, for example raceB or union_typecohab.

Custom functions

Instead of using a formula, users can create a custom function with fun. fun(members, bin) receives a tibble with one row per eligible member of the chosen cell, holding the variables above for every declared dimension (with labels for categorical variables) and identifiers (person_id, or union_id, wife_id and husband_id), and a list bin describing the cell: its process, strata (each dimension's category, or <dim>_w/<dim>_h for union processes, NA when the rates do not stratify by it; origin and destination for transitions), band (age_start/age_end or dur_start/dur_end) and the active rate period time_start/time_end (NA for static rates). Exact ages and times are not passed. In fertility with weighted matching calibration, the function is evaluated at every refresh of every woman, which can be slow.

Time-varying weights

A process's weights may instead be a tibble with numeric time_start, time_end and a list column model of weight models, as for matching and inheritance model schedules.

Examples

# allow mortality to be 10% lower for individuals with partners
partnered_mortality <- weight_model(~partnered, c(partnered = log(0.9)))

# allow dissolution rates to change by 5% per year increase in partner
# age differences - not in absolute terms which would require the custom
# function
gap_dissolution <- weight_model(
  ~age_difference,
  c(age_difference = log(1.05))
)
# like previous example but use custom function to get absolute age
# difference
gap_dissolution <- weight_model(
  fun = function(members, bin) {
    log(1.05) * abs(members$age_difference)
  }
)
